newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: G10 forecasts growth, sees no further gold sales.
newsitem.headline: G10 forecasts growth, sees no further gold sales.

text.p: Top industrial nations should enjoy economic growth in 1997 and 1998 and their central banks see no need to sell gold reserves to boost national revenues, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Monday.
But Tietmeyer noted that Europe must still tackle the structural problems causing the region's high unemployment.

"The latest forecasts continue to suggest a modest acceleration of real growth this year as far as the G10 group is concerned," Tietmeyer told reporters after central bankers from the Group of 10 held a monthly meeting in Basle.
The German banker, who chairs the G10 central bankers committee, said it was expected that this acceleration would be "sustained" in 1998.

As Monday's meeting got under way, the Dutch central bank announced it sold 300 tonnes of gold last year, raising about 6.4 billion guilders ($3.60 billion) which it will hold as interest-bearing foreign currency reserves.
Rumours of a sale from a central bank of around 10 million ounces (300 tonnes) had been current in the market for weeks and were a key factor behind gold's loss of value late last year.
Holding foreign exchange instead of gold will lead to an annual increase of 250 million guilders in the profits that the Dutch central bank bank transfers to the government.

The sale is the Netherlands' second major gold divestment since it sold 400 tonnes in 1992. That news came on the heels of a 200-tonne Belgian sale in the same year. Belgium subsequently sold 175 tonnes in 1995 and a further 203 tonnes in the first quarter of 1996.
But Tietmeyer said other countries were unlikely to follow suit in a bid to plug fiscal deficits and qualify this year as founding members of Europe's single currency in 1999.

"For the time being, there is no intention for (G10) central banks to sell gold," Tietmeyer said. He said there was no "formal agreement" on gold sales but noted that those attending the meeting indicated they had no such intentions.
Tietmeyer gave an upbeat review of the global economy, but said unemployment and the structural problems causing it were still the most difficult economic challenge in Europe.
"Of course strong growth rates will improve the situation, but the growth alone cannot solve it. The structural problems have to be addressed in Europe," Tietmeyer said.
Central bankers also concluded that there was no cause for concern about foreign exchange rates in Europe and that inflation within member countries was still in check.
Despite its name, the G10 groups 11 countries -- the United States, Japan, Germany, France, Britain, Italy, Canada, the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden, and Switzerland.
"All in all, inflation seems to be in practically all countries under control, and monetary policy seems to be in most countries appropriate," Tietmeyer said.
"I haven't heard any concern about the present situation, at least as far as relationship inside Europe and between the dollar and the European area is concerned," he added.
In addition, Tietmeyer said that the Group of 10 discussed the situation in Japanese financial markets, but he declined to specify whether they had drawn any conclusions.
"We have discussed that, but it is up to the Japanese to say how they see it," he said.

The Tokyo stock market's main barometer, the 225-share Nikkei average, lost more than 2,000 points last week on increasing worries about the government's ability to keep economic recovery on track and fulfil promises of vital reforms.

The market bounced back somewhat on Monday, but brokers in Tokyo described the advance as mostly technical. The Nikkei average rose 815.14 points, or 4.71 percent, on Monday to finish at 18,118.79. ($1=1.779 Guilder)
